Where it began

Vangipurapu Venkata Sai Laxman was born in Hyderabad on 1 November 1974 and went to Little Flower High School in the city. He started a medical degree before deciding that cricket was the career for him, which cost the world a doctor and gave it a batsman. His first-class debut for Hyderabad brought a duck, but runs for India Under-19 soon followed, and in the 1999–2000 Ranji Trophy season he made 1,415 runs with eight hundreds, a record for a single season.

The player

Laxman played 134 Tests for India from 1996 to 2012. He scored 8,781 runs at 45.97, with 17 hundreds and 56 fifties, and held 134 catches. Of all Test cricketers he ranks 16th for matches played and 16th for catches.

One innings defines him. At Kolkata in 2001 India followed on against an Australian side that had won 16 Tests in a row. Laxman made 281, then the highest score by an Indian, and with Rahul Dravid added 376 while they batted through the whole fourth day. India won the match and the series, and Wisden later placed the innings sixth among the greatest ever played. Australia remained his favourite opponents: six of his Test hundreds came against them, and both his double-centuries. At Mohali in 2010, with India 124 for 8 chasing 216, he stayed to the end on 73 not out and saw them home by one wicket.

What made him special

He batted with his wrists. He could hit the same ball to either side of the field, drive a big-spinning leg-break against the turn through the off side, and find gaps that fielders thought they had closed. Usually batting at five or six, he became a master at farming the tail and turning a lost position into a draw or a win, which is why he gathered the nickname 'God of the 4th Innings'. He was also a superb catcher close to the bat.

Running between the wickets was not his favourite part of the game. Nobody ever mistook him for a sprinter, but then nobody needed to run many of the ones he stroked to the boundary.

Away from the middle

He was one of Wisden's Cricketers of the Year in 2002, received the Arjuna Award and, in 2011, the Padma Shri. He captained the Deccan Chargers in the first season of the Indian Premier League, later mentored Sunrisers Hyderabad, and sat on the Indian board's Cricket Advisory Committee with Sachin Tendulkar and Sourav Ganguly. He went on to head cricket at the National Cricket Academy and to coach India's Under-19 and A teams. When he retired, Hyderabad's Test ground named its northern stand after him.

And finally

During one tour of Australia, Ian Chappell decided that VVS stood for Very Very Special. Bowlers who spent a day at Eden Gardens trying to stop him would not have argued: he made 1,217 runs on that ground, at an average of 110.63.
